findings.statement: with sequential keys recycling WAL files lifts durable ingest by at least 1.10x
findings.detail: 123037 ops/s recycled against 503985 fresh (recycle vs fresh: less 0.244x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 5.3%/13.4%)); commit phase 0.009s against 0.011s, seal 0.012s against 0.012s, merge 0.011s against 0.010s. Every commit's fdatasync lands in blocks already allocated and written, so no inode change rides the barrier

findings.statement: recycling costs at most 1.05x the device bytes under either key order
findings.detail: device bytes: uniform 73.2 MB recycled against 9.2 fresh (7.958x), sequential 73.2 against 9.2 (7.958x); disk after close: uniform 35.3 against 3.3 MB, sequential 35.3 against 3.3. The pool pre-writes two files of seal size once

findings.statement: with uniform keys recycling lifts durable ingest by at least 1.10x
findings.detail: 120456 ops/s recycled against 485000 fresh (recycle vs fresh: less 0.248x (p=0.0122, rel_iqr 7.8%/3.4%)); commit phase 0.009s against 0.012s, merge 0.011s against 0.011s

findings.statement: reads after the drain do not differ with recycling under either key order
findings.detail: uniform: 123 ns per read recycled against 117 (recycle vs fresh: NO DIFFERENCE (ratio 1.059, p=0.1735) -- within noise, not a result); sequential: 135 against 114 (recycle vs fresh: greater 1.179x (p=0.0051, rel_iqr 5.1%/2.4%)). Nothing on the read path knows what a WAL file looked like

notes: four arms interleaved in one process, fresh store per rep, defaults otherwise (32 MB seals, 64 MB partitions, Sync::Always, one commit per batch) with the drain inside the window. Two key orders, uniform and sequential; WAL files fresh per rotation, or recycled from a pre-written pool so every commit's fdatasync is an overwrite. Device and disk bytes, phases, and point reads after the drain
